speaker: Craig Fuller
title: We're In the Midst of Trucking Bloodbath 2.0
question: In freight transportation, why does trucking experience much more extreme boom-and-bust capacity cycles than industries like commercial airlines?
guest: There's no barriers to entry. A used truck can be anywhere from $50,000 to $100,000, and banks are happy to lend to trucking companies because they have this perception that trucking's always needed. Because they believe there's a perpetual driver shortage, they increasingly provide capital for would-be owner-operators to go out and start their own trucking company. And because of the proliferation of load boards and digital matching apps, it's never been easier to actually access freight and access the brokerage market. New entrepreneurs look at it and say, 'I don't have to be that sophisticated to run a business, and it's incredibly easy to get started.' At the peak of $4 a mile, a truck doing 2,000 miles a week is making $350,000 to $400,000 a year without any formal education or tenure required. So it attracted a lot of folks who weren't cut out for the down cycle. Used five-year-old trucks that used to be $40,000 went for $140,000 to $150,000—more than a new truck pre-COVID. They bought at the top of the market, anticipated that $4-a-mile rate staying perpetual, and were not prepared for the downturn.

points.core: Trucking has virtually zero barriers to entry for new operators.
points.note: Accept: low startup cost, relatively cheap used trucks, no formal degree or tenure required, easy to open a trucking authority. Do not credit: vague statements about competition without explaining low entry barriers.

points.core: Lenders eagerly finance new trucks assuming freight demand stays perpetual.
points.note: Accept: banks readily lend to owner-operators believing in a permanent driver shortage or constant trucking demand. Do not credit: generic mentions of interest rates or credit markets without linking to peak-cycle entry.

points.core: Digital load boards let inexperienced entrants immediately access brokered freight.
points.note: Accept: freight-matching apps or load boards remove the need for sales sophistication or established shipper relationships. Do not credit: generic references to technology or software improving logistics.

points.core: Boom rates lure newcomers into buying overpriced equipment before downturns.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Trucking's cycles are more violent mainly because the industry is extremely fragmented and has very low barriers to entry and exit, so capacity responds quickly and in an uncoordinated way to price signals.

In the US, hundreds of thousands of carriers operate, and the vast majority run only a handful of trucks. When spot rates spike, anyone with a commercial licence can lease or finance a truck, get operating authority cheaply, and start hauling within weeks. Thousands of small operators do this at once, each responding to the same high rates, and existing fleets order new trucks too. That capacity arrives after demand has peaked, producing a glut. Rates then collapse, often below operating cost, and the thinly capitalised small carriers fail or leave, tightening capacity until the next upswing.

Airlines, by contrast, are a concentrated oligopoly with enormous capital requirements, long aircraft order lead times, limited airport slots and gates, and heavy regulatory hurdles. A few large players can see each other's moves and practise capacity discipline, so supply adjusts slowly and deliberately.

Trucking is also a largely undifferentiated commodity priced partly on a volatile spot market, which amplifies the swings.

points.why: Cheap operating authority and a short time to start hauling establish low barriers to entry.
quotes: anyone with a commercial licence can lease or finance a truck, get operating authority cheaply, and start hauling within weeks

points.why: The response mentions financing during rate spikes without linking lenders’ willingness to lend to expectations of persistent freight demand or a driver shortage.
The response gives no mechanism by which load boards or freight-matching apps help new operators access brokered freight.
The response links peak rates to entry and oversupply but omits newcomers overpaying for equipment in the expectation that peak rates would last.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Trucking experiences far more volatile capacity cycles than commercial airlines primarily because of extreme market fragmentation and low barriers to entry. Major airlines operate as a consolidated oligopoly constrained by multibillion-dollar capital requirements, strict regulatory certification, scarce airport slots, and multiyear aircraft and pilot pipelines. By contrast, the truckload sector consists of hundreds of thousands of independent owner-operators and small fleets. When freight demand surges and spot rates spike, new entrants flood in—financing or leasing used trucks and securing operating authority within weeks—while established carriers aggressively order new tractors. Because countless price-taking operators expand simultaneously without visibility into aggregate supply, capacity routinely overshoots demand, compounding the glut once backlogged factory truck orders finally deliver. When freight volumes cool, capacity exits painfully slowly: locked into fixed truck payments and insurance costs, small carriers keep hauling loads near variable cash cost just to service debt, driving rates down until insolvencies force them out. Consolidated airlines, conversely, exercise centralized supply discipline, parking aircraft and trimming flight frequencies to protect yields rather than racing prices to the bottom.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Trucking swings more because it's very easy to get in and out of, and no one in it controls total capacity.

Starting a trucking company takes a commercial driver's license, operating authority that can be issued in weeks, and a financed or used tractor costing roughly $150,000. Most US carriers run ten or fewer trucks, and many are owner-operators. When spot rates rise, as they did in 2020–21, thousands of new entrants and new truck orders arrive within months. The work is close to a commodity and there are no gates or slots to limit it, so capacity overshoots demand. Rates then collapse, and capacity leaves slowly as small carriers burn through savings, default on truck loans, or go back to driving for larger fleets. That lag is what produced the long freight recession of 2022–24.

Airlines face much more friction. Planes cost tens of millions of dollars, and Boeing and Airbus have order backlogs that run for years. Airport slots, gates, and safety certification are tightly limited. After years of mergers, a few large carriers dominate and actively hold capacity down. Airline supply can't flood in quickly, so their cycles are milder.

points.why: The response identifies quick operating authorization as a concrete reason trucking is easy to enter.

operating authority that can be issued in weeks

The response does not explain how load boards or freight-matching apps give newcomers immediate access to brokered freight.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Trucking experiences far more extreme boom-and-bust cycles than commercial airlines because it combines very low barriers to entry with extreme market fragmentation and sticky capacity exits.

When freight rates surge, new capacity floods in rapidly. Unlike airlines—which face massive capital requirements, scarce airport slots, and multi-year aircraft delivery backlogs—trucking lets thousands of small carriers and owner-operators enter the market quickly with a commercial license and a financed rig. Because the industry is fragmented across hundreds of thousands of small firms rather than a handful of disciplined oligopolists, nobody coordinates supply, causing capacity to routinely overshoot demand.

Once rates fall, however, excess trucks leave the market painfully slowly. Fixed truck payments and insurance push struggling carriers to keep hauling near or below break-even just to sustain cash flow, prolonging the glut until widespread bankruptcies finally force capacity out. Airlines, by contrast, operate in a concentrated market with high entry barriers and slow fleet growth, enabling far tighter capacity discipline through downturns.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Trucking capacity is easy for any one carrier to add, which makes it easy for the industry as a whole to add too much. The industry is fragmented, and an owner-operator can enter with a single financed or leased truck. When freight demand rises and spot rates jump, thousands of operators respond to the same price signal. By the time the extra trucks and drivers are on the road, demand may already be cooling.

Once there are more trucks than loads, spot rates fall quickly. Carriers with truck payments still due may keep hauling as long as a load covers the immediate cost of running it, even if the rate won’t cover their total costs. That delays the withdrawal of capacity. As carriers finally exit, the market can tighten sharply when demand recovers.

Commercial airlines are more concentrated and face higher barriers to entry. Aircraft, trained crews, airport access, and scheduled networks take substantial capital and planning. Airlines can adjust flight frequencies, but those constraints limit the rush of new capacity when fares rise.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra

Trucking capacity is easy to add one truck at a time. When freight demand rises faster than the available fleet, shippers bid up rates. High rates draw in owner-operators and prompt existing carriers to order trucks. Each carrier responds to the same price signal, and new trucks can arrive just as demand cools. Rates then fall sharply. Capacity takes longer to leave because a carrier may keep hauling as long as a load covers its immediate costs, even if the rate is too low to sustain the business.

Airlines face much higher barriers to entry. Aircraft are expensive, certification takes time, and airport gates can be scarce. A relatively small number of carriers also control most capacity, and each can adjust flight frequency across its network. Airlines still have cycles, but a surge in fares is less likely to trigger a wave of independent entrants that leaves the market oversupplied.
